title: Counting steps
summary: Count how many times code looks at an item, and see O(1) and O(n).

say.never: How fast is a piece of code? Seconds depend on the computer, so programmers count **steps** instead: here, how many times the code looks at an item in a list. A playlist has `n` songs. Asking for the song at a spot, like `songs.get(4)`, is one look. A list can jump straight to any spot, so it's one look whether the playlist has 10 songs or 10,000.
say.bit: Measure speed in **steps**, not seconds: how many items the code looks at. `get(i)` on a list is one step, however long the list is.

board.code:
String first = songs.get(0);
String fifth = songs.get(4);

say.never: Code that takes the same number of steps no matter how big `n` is, is called **O(1)**, said "order one" or **constant time**. Grabbing the first song is O(1). So is grabbing the last one, because you can work out where the end is: the list's `size()` tells you, without looking at any songs.
say.bit: Same steps for any `n` is **O(1)**, constant time. `size()` doesn't look at items, so jumping to the end is O(1) too.

board.code:
int count = songs.size();
String middle = songs.get(count / 2);

say.never: Now find the longest song. There's no way to know without checking every one, so a loop looks at each song once. Double the playlist and the loop does double the work. That straight-line growth is **O(n)**, "order n" or **linear time**.
say.bit: One look per item is **O(n)**, linear: double `n`, double the steps.

say.never: `latest` wants the most recent score, which is the last one in the list. Don't loop to get there: work out its spot from `size()` and jump straight to it. That's O(1). Check for an empty list first, because an empty list has no last spot. `best` has to see every score, so it's one loop: O(n). The checker counts your looks on a list of 1500 scores.
say.bit: `latest`: check empty, then jump to the last spot (O(1)). `best`: one loop over every score (O(n)).
